 MSFT Stock Reverses and Heads to $500 After Microsoft 365 Services Impacted by Outlook Outage
 Microsoft shares retreat toward $520 after a service disruption affects Outlook, Teams, Copilot and Microsoft 365, adding another source of uncertainty as investors reassess rising infrastructure costs, competition from Anthropic and the profitability of cloud expansion.
 Written by: 
 Skerdian Meta 
 • 
 Thursday, November 12, 2026 
 • 
 3 min read 
 • 
 Last updated: Thursday, November 12, 2026 
 Add an article to your Reading List Register now to be able to add articles to your reading list. SIGN UP Already have an account? Sign in " aria-hidden="true"> 
 Quick overview
 Microsoft shares have fallen toward $520 following a service disruption affecting Outlook, Teams, and Microsoft 365, raising investor concerns.
 The outage led to over 130,000 reports of issues with Outlook and highlighted the reliance on Microsoft's cloud services.
 Investors are increasingly worried about rising infrastructure costs and competition from Anthropic's new workplace software.
 Despite strong earnings, there are growing doubts about the profitability of Microsoft's cloud expansion and its ability to generate sufficient returns.
 Microsoft shares retreat toward $520 after a service disruption affects Outlook, Teams, Copilot and Microsoft 365, adding another source of uncertainty as investors reassess rising infrastructure costs, competition from Anthropic and the profitability of cloud expansion. 
 Microsoft Stock Falls Toward $520 After Global Outage
 Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares have extended their retreat from record highs near $560, falling toward $520 as investors confront another setback for the technology giant. The stock had recovered sharply from the $500 area following the U.S. midterm elections, but renewed concerns about infrastructure spending, competition and operational reliability have weakened sentiment.
 Thursday’s decline accelerated after disruptions affected several Microsoft services, including Outlook, Teams, Copilot and Microsoft 365. Users reported difficulties accessing email, workplace collaboration tools and other cloud-based applications, while Microsoft warned that the disruption could affect service connectivity across multiple regions.
 Downdetector recorded more than 130,000 reports of Outlook problems at 1:27 p.m. ET, alongside more than 46,000 reports involving Microsoft 365 and approximately 3,000 concerning Teams. These figures represent user-submitted reports rather than confirmed numbers of affected customers.
 Microsoft initially said it had resolved a Teams disruption affecting North American users, but subsequently indicated that the wider connectivity issue could affect Microsoft 365 customers internationally.
 Although temporary service disruptions do not necessarily indicate a structural problem, the incident highlights the dependence of businesses on Microsoft’s cloud-based productivity ecosystem.
 Data-Centre Expansion Adds to Investor Concerns
 The outage comes as Microsoft faces growing scrutiny over the cost and scale of its infrastructure expansion.
 Noelle Walsh, President of Cloud Operations and Innovation, reiterated that Microsoft would finance its own data-centre construction and associated infrastructure. Her comments extend a community-first commitment announced in January 2026, under which the company pledged to cover electricity costs and grid upgrades associated with its projects rather than transferring those expenses to local residents.
 Walsh oversees Microsoft’s global data-centre operations, managing approximately 15,000 employees and a multibillion-dollar investment programme.
 While covering infrastructure costs could reduce community opposition and regulatory friction, it also reinforces the financial burden associated with expanding Azure and computing capacity.
 Investors increasingly want evidence that additional infrastructure can generate sufficient revenue without weakening margins and free cash flow.
 Anthropic Challenges Microsoft’s Productivity Business
 Competition is another emerging concern after Anthropic introduced workplace software targeting markets dominated by Microsoft and Google.
 Its products include a videoconferencing assistant, data dashboards and Claude Sheets, a spreadsheet service positioned against Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets. The company also plans to allow enterprises to integrate existing applications into Claude, potentially turning the platform into a central interface for workplace activities.
 This represents a competitive challenge for Microsoft’s productivity ecosystem.
 Microsoft 365 Cloud generated $27.78 billion in first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue, ended September 30, 2026, increasing approximately 17% year-over-year and accounting for around 30% of total company revenue.
 Although this includes broader commercial and consumer cloud services, it demonstrates the importance of the productivity business to Microsoft’s financial performance.
 MSFT Stock Reverses Lower
 Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months which has now turned into a support zone, and climbed above $550 earlier in October but slipped toward $500 again on Monday. The price slip breached the 50 daily SMA in September which has been acting as support and we’re seeing a rebound today. The price has now pushed to a new record high above $555 area which represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MSFT buyers gave up at this zone, reversing lower below $520 today.
 MSFT Chart Daily – Returning Toward the 20 SMA 
 Strong Earnings Fail to Remove Spending Concerns
 Microsoft’s latest quarterly results remained impressive. Net income increased 32% year-over-year to $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, while revenue climbed to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier.
 Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year-over-year, or 31% in constant currency.
 However, strong earnings have not eliminated concerns about the capital required to maintain growth. Data centres, servers, networking equipment and specialised processors require substantial upfront investment, and investors increasingly want measurable returns rather than larger spending commitments.
 $44.9 Billion Anthropic Commitment and Maia 300
 An amended filing concerning Microsoft’s relationship with Anthropic identifies at least $44.9 billion in commitments through June 2033, subject to contractual delivery and breach provisions.
 Microsoft is also developing its Maia 300 custom processor, reportedly targeting 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems. Its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to improve rack-scale computing capacity.
 Custom silicon could eventually reduce computing costs and dependence on external suppliers, but development and deployment require additional investment before those efficiency gains translate into stronger profitability.
 Microsoft Stock Outlook: $520 Support in Focus
 Microsoft’s latest retreat reflects several overlapping concerns: service reliability, rising infrastructure costs, Anthropic’s competitive expansion and questions about future returns.
 The company’s strong earnings and cloud growth remain important positives, but investors are becoming increasingly selective about the financial benefits of expanding computing capacity.
 With MSFT retreating from $560 toward $520, the immediate technical focus shifts to whether buyers can defend the $520 area. A sustained recovery will require renewed buying interest and stronger confidence that Microsoft’s infrastructure investments can deliver profitable growth without undermining free cash flow.
